articles.title: Your setTimeout Didn't Break — Chrome Killed It
articles.excerpt: The log said the sync was scheduled. Two minutes later, nothing had run. No error, no rejected promise, no missed callback warning — just a line that promised future work and a database that never cha…
articles.body: The log said the sync was scheduled. Two minutes later, nothing had run. No error, no rejected promise, no missed callback warning — just a line that promised future work and a database that never changed. Here is the excerpt that ended a week of blaming my own debounce logic: [10:41:02] change detected [10:41:02] sync scheduled in 120000ms [10:41:32] service worker terminated (idle) The timer did not fail. The process that owned it was shut down, and a setTimeout cannot outlive its process. The short version setTimeout is a handle in the worker's heap. Terminate the worker and the handle is gone. MV3 kills an idle background worker after about 30 seconds, no matter what is pending. Persist the due time , not the timer, and re-arm it when the worker wakes.

articles.title: Git security vulnerabilities announced
articles.excerpt: Git is releasing updates addressing six security vulnerabilities affecting recursive clones, reference handling, merges, binary patches, and imports. Here is what users need to know. The post Git secu…
articles.body: Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches. The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1 , with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git. Vulnerabilities in Git CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata.

articles.title: 6 Planning Patterns for AI Agents and When Each One Fits
articles.excerpt: TL;DR for devs Start from the task, not from a popular reasoning pattern. Use a fixed workflow for predictable steps; consider model-generated plans when tasks vary. Other patterns: plan then execute,…
articles.body: TL;DR for devs Start from the task, not from a popular reasoning pattern. Use a fixed workflow for predictable steps; consider model-generated plans when tasks vary. Other patterns: plan then execute, ReAct-style tool use, routing to specialists, parallel work, and draft-evaluate-revise. A plan is a proposal, not a guarantee, so validate actions and results. Set stopping conditions (max steps, time limits) and let code handle exact arithmetic and rules.

articles.title: Were there 'lost cosmonauts' in the early Soviet space program?
articles.excerpt: At the height of the Cold War, two amateur radio operators alleged they intercepted signals from Soviet cosmonauts who perished during missions that remained secret.
articles.body: In the final weeks of 1960, two young radio enthusiasts were monitoring transmissions from a home-built listening station on a rooftop in Turin, Italy, when the brothers detected something extraordinary: a faint signal that bore the hallmarks of one originating from space. That wasn't the only surprising thing about the alleged signal:, the transmission carried a very familiar message: it was Morse code for the international distress signal SOS. As the youths listened, the signal seemed to grow weaker. This raised a troubling possibility: could it be that the signal's source was moving farther away from Earth ?

articles.title: NASA Scientists Show How Gravitational Waves Can Reveal New Worlds
articles.excerpt: The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory, now in development, will detect gravitational waves, the tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses. Now two studies led by NASA as…
articles.body: 5 min read NASA Scientists Show How Gravitational Waves Can Reveal New Worlds The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory, now in development, will detect gravitational waves, the tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses. Now two studies led by NASA astrophysicists show in new detail how LISA could reveal a new and unique population of exoplanets — worlds beyond our solar system — throughout our galaxy. Watch to learn how the presence of a planet modifies the gravitational wave signal from tightly orbiting white dwarfs. The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory could detect a Jupiter-mass planet in such systems up to thousands of light-years away.

articles.body: A robot just played Tinkertoys in space, assembling the first satellite structure ever made without a human touching the controls. The DARPA-funded project saw a robotic "truss builder" create a reflective antenna using Kapton film, composite fiber tubes and aluminum joints. The implications are huge for future missions, potentially opening up new possibilities to build — or fix — satellites in the final frontier. "This is the first time that a structure has been autonomously constructed in space ," Sergio Pellegrino, an aerospace and civil engineering professor at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement on Nov. 5 .

articles.body: NASA’s Mars rover Curiosity acquired this close-up image using its Mars Hand Lens Imager, showing the abundance of disc-shaped potential crystal forms on our next drill target, dubbed "Nazca." (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS) NASA's Curiosity Mars rover is sizing up its next dig site on the Red Planet. The Curiosity team will characterize the surface composition of the Mars site, informally named "Nazca," as thoroughly as possible before drilling into it. What is it? Curiosity snapped the close-up image on Oct. 18, 2026, using its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI). articles.body: As rival makers announce increasingly ambitious smart telescopes , ZWO has taken a different approach. Its new Seestar S30 Plus launched today and is available for $474 from Seestar’s website and Amazon , just in time for Christmas. Better still, we’ve been using it for a month and can bring you a first look. Announced a few months after the flagship Seestar S50 Pro and replacing the now-discontinued Seestar S30 , the new Seestar S30 Plus retains its 30mm aperture and compact chassis, but upgrades to four-element apochromatic optics with extra-low dispersion (ED) glass and two 3.7-megapixel cameras. The ZWO Seestar S30 Plus is a new sub-$500 smart telescope with upgraded optics and dual 3.7MP cameras.
